newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -TIGHT U.S. SUPPLY TAKES BACK SEAT.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -TIGHT U.S. SUPPLY TAKES BACK SEAT.

text.p: What could have sold like hot cakes a week ago turned out to be unappetising for investors in this week's U.S. Treasury quarterly refunding.

But despite concerns about possible increases in economic growth, few markets could match the U.S., with many European governments struggling to fit their deficits into the single currency corset of a three percent-to-GDP ratio, analysts said on Friday.

"The market lost its bottle after the 30-year auction on Thursday," said George Magnus, chief international economist at UBS in London. But he added Treasuries would continue to outperform Bunds with the spread expected to shrink to 50 basis points.
The 10-year U.S./German spread was at 71 basis points by 1306 GMT.
The Treasury's $38 billion quarterly refunding this week failed to generate the level of demand that was anticipated with a chunk of the paper yet to be placed with end-buyers.
The $10 billion auction averaged a yield of 6.445 percent with a stop at 6.452.
With Bunds overshadowed by rate hike fears and yield-hungry investors in Japan, the bid-to-cover ratio could have been significantly better than around 2.40, analysts said.
Magnus said the market would tread water for a while to digest the new issue after its dive on stronger than expected data last Friday.
Many economists were forecasting a more robust third quarter for the U.S. economy after three soggy months which wiped the threat of inflation from the agenda.
"I suspect the next stop for the long bond is probably 6.75 percent by end-September, October," said Dick Howard, senior economist at Bank Julius Baer in London.
The 30-year bond is currently yielding 6.5 percent.
"Cyclical factors will certainly overwhelm structural factors on a two to three month view," Howard said.
"The consensus story now is third quarter growth will be around 3.0-3.5 percent (from 2.2 in Q2)," he said, adding that such growth levels could warrant a Federal Reserve rate hike in September.
Howard saw the T-note/Bund spread widening to around 75 basis points.
Magnus pointed to July retail sales, due on Wednesday, for fresh guidance.

"If in July we have 0.7 percent or higher and June is revised up, this has the capacity to change the direction," he said, forecasting the long bond yield at between 7.00-7.25 percent by the year end.
Michael Derks, cross market fixed income strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, said the auction disappointment could haunt the market for a while.

"There is a whole myriad of corporate paper that's going into the street each week," he said, referring to U.S. defence contractor Raytheon's $3.0 billion debt offering on Thursday that had also weighed on the market.
But supply could be absorbed even if the demand side of the economy remained jaded, analysts said.
"There is still a lot of cash around. One forgets that there are 23 billion dollars worth of maturities coming through in August and an enormous level of coupon payments," Derks said.
